definitions.definition: A measure of how many different ways you can arrange the tiny parts of a system and still get the same overall look.
definitions.example: Think of a messy desk: there are many ways to scatter papers (high entropy) vs. a perfectly organized desk (low entropy).

definitions.definition: The specific, detailed arrangement of every tiny particle in a system.
definitions.example: For a deck of cards, each unique order of the 52 cards is a microstate.

definitions.definition: The big-picture description of a system, ignoring tiny details.
definitions.example: Saying 'the room is hot' is a macrostate; the exact speeds of every air molecule are microstates.

definitions.definition: A rule that says if there is too much random interference (noise) in a communication channel, the message gets destroyed.
definitions.example: Trying to talk on a phone with terrible static — if the static is too loud, you can't understand anything.

definitions.definition: When something grows faster and faster because each step adds to the previous step in a multiplying way.
definitions.example: A rumor that doubles every hour: 1, 2, 4, 8, 16... it explodes quickly.

definitions.definition: Claiming that something's very nature or existence is the same as something else.
definitions.example: Saying 'I am love' means your whole being is love, not just that you feel love sometimes.

definitions.definition: The basic 'stuff' that has no disorder at all — perfectly organized.
definitions.example: Imagine a perfectly clean room where every item has exactly one place and nothing is out of order.

definitions.definition: The idea that evil is not a real thing, but just the absence or lack of good.
definitions.example: Darkness isn't a thing; it's just the absence of light. Similarly, evil is the absence of good.

definitions.definition: Related to the mathematical study of information, signals, and noise.
definitions.example: Thinking about a conversation in terms of how much information gets through vs. how much is lost or garbled.

definitions.definition: A perfect one-to-one match between two different things, where the structure is preserved.
definitions.example: A map of a subway system and the actual subway lines: each station on the map matches a real station, and connections match.

definitions.definition: A set of rules to find and fix mistakes in a message or system.
definitions.example: When you text someone and it says 'did you mean...?' that's a simple error-correction.

definitions.definition: Mixing up where a signal or message actually comes from.
definitions.example: Thinking a rumor came from a reliable friend when it actually started from a gossip website.

definitions.definition: A way to shrink data by throwing away some details, making it less accurate.
definitions.example: A blurry photo saved as a small file — it looks okay but you lost fine details.

definitions.definition: Putting the wrong name or address on a communication line.
definitions.example: Writing the wrong email address so your message goes to the wrong person.

definitions.definition: When two systems' timing gets out of sync, causing errors.
definitions.example: Two people trying to sing a duet but one is off-beat — the song falls apart.

definitions.definition: When a message gets corrupted because a middle person or device messes it up.
definitions.example: Playing telephone: the last person hears a completely different sentence than the first person said.

definitions.definition: Breaking the device or person that is supposed to receive the message.
definitions.example: Smashing your phone so you can't get any texts — no signal can get through.

definitions.definition: When signals from two different communication lines mix together.
definitions.example: Hearing someone else's conversation faintly on your phone line.

definitions.definition: Using up communication capacity that was meant for someone else.
definitions.example: Someone streaming a movie on your Wi-Fi without permission, slowing down your internet.

definitions.definition: Adding fake information into a communication channel.
definitions.example: Hacking a news website to post a false story.

definitions.definition: Mistakes or bad thoughts that happen before a message is even sent.
definitions.example: Thinking of a lie and then deciding to tell it — the noise starts in your own mind.

definitions.definition: Keeping the same pattern or relationships when mapping one thing to another.
definitions.example: A chess board and a diagram of it: the positions and moves are the same, just drawn differently.

definitions.definition: The property that a mapping is forced by logic, not chosen randomly.
definitions.example: 2+2=4 is not arbitrary; it's forced by the rules of math.

definitions.definition: When two things predict each other — each one gives information about the other.
definitions.example: If rain makes the ground wet, then seeing wet ground tells you it rained. That's bidirectional.

definitions.definition: A perfect match in structure between two different systems.
definitions.example: The rules of addition for numbers and the rules for adding lengths on a ruler are structurally isomorphic.

definitions.definition: Specific conditions that, if true, would prove a scientific claim wrong.
definitions.example: If you claim 'all swans are white,' then finding one black swan is a falsification criterion.

definitions.definition: Lowering the status of a match from a perfect structural match to just a general similarity.
definitions.example: Saying a map is 'like' the territory (correspondence) vs. saying it is structurally identical (isomorphism).

definitions.definition: A comparison showing similarity between two things, but not a perfect match.
definitions.example: Saying 'the heart is like a pump' is an analogy.

definitions.definition: Limits or rules that must be followed for a system to work properly.
definitions.example: A bridge must be strong enough to hold cars — that's an engineering constraint.

definitions.definition: Related to the nature of existence or being.
definitions.example: Asking 'does God exist?' is an ontological question.
